extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and researchers of Holocaust/Auschwitz history
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedia article describing the systems, rules, practices, and resistance related to censorship (mail, art, and communication) in Auschwitz concentration camp during the Third Reich. It summarizes administrative structures, regulations, examples, and postwar preservation of censored materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence format and content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters had to be legibly written in ink, no more than 15 lines per page, on uniformly distributed camp stationery; only one sheet of standard letterhead was permitted. Postcards must be written in 10 lines. Letters had to be signed with the sender's name and the belonged camp's name, put in standard envelopes with a Geprüft stamp, and include the opening phrase 'I am healthy and feel well' (German: 'Ich bin gesund und fühle mich gut').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: only 5 stamps of 12 pence may be enclosed; photographs may not be used as postcards; sending money is permitted but enclosures otherwise prohibited; exact address must include name, date of birth, and prisoner number or the correspondence will be returned or destroyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on who may correspond
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a small number of German- and Polish-ethnic prisoners were allowed to write and send correspondences. Unregistered prisoners and prisoners with the designation 'Nacht und Nebel' (NN), including Soviet POWs, Jewish and half-Jewish prisoners, and prisoners whose families lived in non-Nazi jurisdictional areas were excluded from corresponding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations from March 30, 1942, further limited correspondence for people from the East (Ostvölker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on frequency and parcels
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally two letters or postcards were allowed to be sent every month per prisoner. For people from the East, only one letter every two months was permitted. Parcels were not allowed (parcels may not be sent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers were permitted but only via the camp post office; though sending money was allowed, SS personnel often embezzled it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected prisoners were required to write in German, the official language of the Third Reich. Polish, Silesian, and Yiddish were strictly banned for correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This linguistic restriction further limited which prisoners could effectively communicate and increased reliance on German-fluent prisoners as intermediaries or ghostwriters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship enforcement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mail Censorship Office (Postzensurstelle) supervised reception and sending of correspondence and censored contents. SS personnel would cut or blacken suspicious words or sentences; sometimes entire passages would be deleted. Letters containing excessive 'inappropriate' content would be detained and never sent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Division I and II did not officially release clear regulations on content, increasing prisoners' fear; censorship was used to control information about actual camp conditions (starvation, torture, sickness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative oversight and use of records
rubrics_metrics.description: Postzensurstelle was directly subordinated to Division I (the commandant's office) and collaborated with Division II (the political department). The Section for Registration, Organization, and Documentation and the Identification Service kept prisoners' personal records and family addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondence records were used to verify identities and addresses and to detect prisoners registered under false names, helping prevent escapes by threatening family arrests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Briefaktion — forced falsified correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Letter Operation' (Briefaktion) forced Jewish prisoners (notably from Theresienstadt and Berlin) to write and send postcards to their families which falsely stated favorable camp conditions (e.g., 'The food is good', 'We have central heating').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These postcards were used to calm fear about deportation and to deceive recipients and the wider world about the existence and nature of extermination camps; many of these prisoners were later liquidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition and control of artistic production
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating artwork in concentration camps was forbidden unless commanded by camp authorities. 'Commanded art' comprised officially approved works produced under SS commission; clandestine/illegal art was produced secretly and risked harsh punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painting materials were scarce; SS employed prisoner-artists for official tasks (instructional drawings, models, signs) while illegal art circulated on the black market or was smuggled out as documentation and testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege and exploitation tied to assigned roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Prisoners assigned to SS offices, workshops, or as prisoner-functionaries (including artists, housepainters, varnishers) often worked indoors and thus had shelter and relatively better conditions. Prisoner-functionaries were used to convey orders and monitor writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These roles created hierarchies within the camp; SS and prisoner-functionaries exploited resources sent by families and profited from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting and exclusion by ethnicity/status
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship and correspondence privileges were applied unequally: Polish prisoners (early arrivals) often had more opportunity and better jobs; minorities such as Jews, Romani, and Soviet POWs were often unreachable or excluded from services and thus left limited testimonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The system was exclusive and reflected broader Nazi policies of assimilation and racial hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prisoner evasion, self-censorship, and resistance techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Prisoners developed methods to evade censorship: ghostwriting by German-fluent prisoners, 'self-censorship' (writing on one side only), writing in codes or ciphers, using pseudonyms, and employing underground intelligence networks and couriers to smuggle letters, parcels, and information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underground organizations also ran 'letter boxes', safe houses, and courier networks that transmitted food parcels and secret communications to prisoners, though such help was primarily available to Polish and sometimes Czech prisoners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of correspondence as a mechanism of control and deception
rubrics_metrics.description: The correspondence campaign served multiple control purposes: concealing real conditions, deceiving families (via Briefaktion), monitoring recipients, finding false registrations, and discouraging escape by threatening families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censorship thus functioned as both propaganda and a practical security measure for camp administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postwar preservation and evidentiary use of censored materials
rubrics_metrics.description: After liberation, many censored correspondences received by families were donated to the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum and used as historical evidence of censorship practices and camp life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survivor testimonies and preserved letters form part of scholarship and memorialization of camp censorship and daily experience.
